blocks.text: Humans are endothermic homeotherms and regulate body temperature by negative feedback. Thermoreceptors in the skin detect a rise or fall and signal the hypothalamus, which also contains thermoreceptors; the hypothalamus signals muscles and glands to correct it. Thermoreceptors also signal the higher brain centres, so we feel warm or cold and can act, for example by bathing or switching on a fan or heater.

blocks.caption: Human responses
rows: vasodilation: capillaries under the skin widen, more blood flows near the surface and loses heat
vasoconstriction: less blood flows to the skin, so less heat is lost
sweating: evaporation of sweat carries heat away
shivering: spasmodic contraction of skeletal muscles produces heat
the thyroid may secrete less thyroxine, lowering the basal metabolic rate and heat production
goosebumps: hair muscles contract and erect hairs trap insulating air; metabolic rate rises

Bottom left: ammonia, urea and uric acid with about 500, 50 and 1 mL of water per gram as bars. Bottom right: human responses to overheating and to cooling.
blocks.caption: Osmoregulation, nitrogenous wastes and human thermoregulation (original diagram after topics 13.2 and 13.3).
blocks.long_description: A freshwater fish is saltier than the water around it, so water keeps entering by osmosis and salts leak out; it produces a large volume of dilute urine and takes salts back in by active transport, and rarely drinks. A marine bony fish is less salty than sea water, so it loses water and gains salt; it drinks sea water, makes little concentrated urine and uses chloride cells in its gills to pump salt out. Ammonia needs about 500 mL of water per gram to excrete safely, urea about 50 mL and uric acid about 1 mL, so animals short of water excrete urea or uric acid. When the human body is too hot, skin vessels widen and sweat cools it; when it is too cold, skin vessels narrow, muscles shiver and hairs stand up.

blocks.prompt: Describe the regulatory strategies in humans when body temperature rises above 37 C.
blocks.explanation: Skin thermoreceptors signal the hypothalamus; skin capillaries dilate so more heat is lost, sweat glands produce sweat whose evaporation cools the body, and thyroxine secretion may fall to reduce heat production; behaviour such as moving to shade or using a fan also helps.

items: Hot: vasodilation, sweating, less thyroxine. Cold: vasoconstriction, shivering, goosebumps, more metabolism. Control: hypothalamus, negative feedback.
